headline: September inflation ran hot, yet bonds rallied anyway: the 10-year ended the week at 5.09%, 22bp below its Oct 5 peak.
dateline: Monday, October 19, 2026 · closes as of Fri Oct 16

rundown.h: Warsh kept his cards close before next week's meeting.
rundown.p: Speaking to finance officials in Bangkok on Friday, Fed Chair Warsh said he doesn't prejudge meetings and that September's hike removed "a dose of accommodation." He gave no hint on Oct 28. Markets still lean toward a December move: odds of a hike by then were about 89% as of Oct 16.

rundown.h: AI's borrowing binge is showing up in credit spreads.
rundown.p: Mohamed El-Erian flagged that CoreWeave's credit spread spiked to 1,200bp, calling it either a warning sign for tech or a classic overshoot. The Nasdaq lost 4.5% on the week and the S&P 500 2%, while the Dow finished higher. For lenders and allocators, watch whether stress in AI-infrastructure debt spreads to other high-yield borrowers.

rundown.h: Washington waived Russia sanctions to keep diesel flowing.
rundown.p: President Trump signed an order Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the new Graham Act, after a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel; Secretary of State Rubio said the White House will take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact. Brent fell $1.43 to $108.43 in early Monday trade. Cheaper diesel would ease the biggest cost line for truckers.

rundown.h: Regions shows banks lending into the CRE gap.
rundown.p: Regions Financial earned $0.71 a share in Q3, up 16% from a year ago, and net charge-offs fell to 0.29% of loans from 0.42% in Q2. Investor real estate loans grew 9.3% y/y, which management tied to multifamily bridge loans as high long rates stall permanent financing. Fifth Third, Zions and Western Alliance report today; KeyCorp Tuesday; Huntington Thursday.

rundown.h: A heavy week for earnings, from Netflix to the railroads.
rundown.p: Tesla, Netflix, GM and Capital One are due Tuesday, IBM and Texas Instruments Wednesday, and Procter & Gamble, Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern, PulteGroup and NVR Thursday, with American Express and Exxon Mobil on Friday. The railroads and homebuilders give a read on freight volumes and housing demand with mortgages above 7%.

rundown.h: Diesel topped $6 a gallon for a full month.
rundown.p: DAT says September's national diesel average hit $6.291, the first monthly average above $6. Spot dry van averaged $3.01 a mile, up $0.96 from a year ago, and reefer spot set a monthly record at $3.62, even as reefer load volume fell 10% y/y. DAT's Dean Croke says rates usually take three to four weeks to catch up with diesel.

dive.title: The grid is the new bottleneck
dive.dek: Data centers are bidding for electricity faster than the grid can build it, and the bill is landing in capacity prices and power rates.
dive.body:
The U.S. is using more electricity than ever. In its October 6 Short-Term Energy Outlook, the EIA projects consumption of 11.75 billion kWh per day in 2026, up from 11.49 in 2025, rising to 11.94 in 2027. Third-quarter use ran about 4% above a year earlier, helped by a record-hot summer, and EIA expects commercial and industrial demand, the bucket that includes data centers, to grow close to 3% in 2027.

Supply isn't keeping pace, and prices show it. EIA forecasts wholesale power will average $52/MWh in 2026, 11% above 2025, with prices in PJM, the grid from Illinois to New Jersey that holds the densest cluster of data centers, up 41%. Residential rates are on track to rise 5.3% to 18.21¢/kWh. PJM's July capacity auction for 2028/29 cleared at the regulator-imposed cap of $325/MW-day, worth $16.4 billion, and still came up 6,831 MW short of its reliability target. PJM's independent market monitor puts about $6.3 billion of that cost on planned data centers, a bill every ratepayer shares.

Texas shows how far requests run ahead of reality. Reports on ERCOT's large-load queue put it at roughly 474 GW, mostly data centers, more than five times the grid's record peak of about 91 GW set July 22. Only a sliver has cleared the gates to connect, and regulators are now sorting real projects from speculative ones. Utilities are answering with record spending: investor-owned utilities have signaled at least $1.4 trillion of capital spending through 2030, up from a $1.1 trillion five-year plan a year earlier.

For investors and managers, the upshot is that power, not land, increasingly decides where big projects get built and when. Sites with secured interconnection command a premium, utility capex needs financing at today's rates, and every other commercial tenant feels it in rising power bills. What would change the picture: faster interconnection reform, a wave of new gas and storage capacity, or AI spending slowing enough to thin out the queue.

rows: Data centers' share of PJM cost

watch: November EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook: updated power demand and price forecasts.
December: PJM's 2029/30 capacity auction; another clear at the cap would extend the squeeze.

items.title: September CPI: gasoline pushed headline inflation to 3.7%, core edged up to 2.6%

chart.t: CPI, % change from a year earlier
chart.src: Source: BLS via SimianX compilation (Oct 2025 not published, shutdown); Aug–Sep 2026 confirmed by Trading Economics.

items.body:
Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September, in line with forecasts and the biggest monthly gain in five months, lifting the annual rate to 3.7% from 3.4%, above the 3.6% consensus. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% for the month against a 0.2% forecast and 2.6% from a year earlier, up from 2.4%.

Energy did most of the work: gasoline jumped 9.1% in the month and accounted for more than half of the headline increase, leaving it 34.2% higher than a year ago, while fuel oil is up 74.2% y/y. Shelter inflation firmed to 3.2% y/y from 3.0%, and services to 3.2% from 3.1%. Food cooled to 2.5% from 2.7%. Used cars, airfares, apparel and medical care rose; communication fell.

Markets moved, then reversed. Futures-implied odds of an October hike jumped to about 47% right after the release, then fell to roughly 16% by Friday and 14.9% early Monday. The 2-year Treasury rose to 4.82% on release day, then slipped to 4.74% by Friday's close.

experts.view: Kept their call for an October hike, arguing the price gains were broad rather than one-offs.
Expects the Fed to hold for the rest of the year and sees the jump in owners' equivalent rent as possibly a one-month aberration.
Called September's reading an energy shock that should ease once the Iran conflict is resolved.

items.lean: Bank of America expects an October hike; Goldman Sachs and Northlight's Chris Zaccarelli see December instead; Bloomberg Economics expects a hold.

reading.title: Meet Mr. Market
reading.dek: Graham's best-known allegory, from The Intelligent Investor, is a guide to using price swings instead of being pushed around by them.
reading.body:
Benjamin Graham (1894–1976) is often called the father of value investing. Born Benjamin Grossbaum in London, he grew up in New York and taught investing at Columbia Business School for years, where Warren Buffett was one of his students. With David Dodd he wrote Security Analysis (1934), a founding text of the field, and from 1936 until he retired in 1956 he ran the Graham-Newman fund with Jerome Newman. In 1949 he published a shorter, plainer book for non-professionals, The Intelligent Investor, and revised it several times; the last revision, in 1973, drew on Buffett's input, and an annotated edition with commentary by Jason Zweig followed in 2003.

The book's most famous idea is the allegory in chapter 8, on market fluctuations. Imagine you own a small stake in a private business. Your partner, Mr. Market, turns up every day and names a price at which he'll buy your share or sell you his. Some days he's euphoric and asks far too much. Other days he's gloomy and will sell for almost nothing. His moods have little to do with how the business is actually doing.

The point is that his offer is an option, not an instruction. You can take it when it suits you and ignore it when it doesn't. The real mistake is letting his mood set your view of what you own. Sell in a panic because he did, or chase a price because he's excited, and you've handed your judgment to the least reliable person in the room. Graham's investor watches the business itself, its earnings, balance sheet and dividends, rather than the daily quote.

There's comfort in the chapter, too. Graham argued that an investor holding sound assets who isn't forced to sell isn't really harmed by falling prices, and that a falling price can be an opportunity. What matters is keeping price and value separate. That discipline pairs with the other chapter Buffett singles out, on the margin of safety: buy only when the price sits comfortably below a conservative estimate of value, so mistakes and bad luck don't sink you.

Why reread it now? Last week Mr. Market swung from pricing an October Fed hike as a near coin flip to barely considering it, while chip stocks fell sharply in a single session. Graham's framework won't say where markets go next. It asks a simpler question: what are you being paid, and what are you being asked to pay? With a 10-year Treasury near 5%, a safe yield is a real alternative, and a rich price on any asset, stock or building, shrinks the margin of safety.

quote.text: By far the best book on investing ever written.
quote.src: Warren Buffett, on The Intelligent Investor

takeaways: A 5% 10-year sets a real hurdle: an expensive asset has to beat a safe yield, not just its peers.
Fed-odds whiplash makes Mr. Market moody; treat the swings as offers you can take or ignore.
High valuations thin the margin of safety, so ask for a wider discount before buying.
reading.src: Read more: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor (revised edition with commentary by Jason Zweig, 2003), chapter 8; Wikipedia entries on Graham and the book.
